structured.tldr:
Your premise checks out on the record: Chinese business in US soybeans has collapsed this year -- China took 12,357 thousand MT of US beans in MY2025 [N2] against 22,546 [N3] the year before and 24,307 [N4] in MY2023 -- and the weekly sales pace reads behind at 622.69 thousand MT for the week of 10 September 2026 [N66], the 43rd percentile of its own record [N68]. Yet the US balance sheet is NOT loose: the stocks-to-use ratio sits at 10.72% [N54], the 23rd percentile of its own record [N56] and falling three marketing years running, so the net setup points toward higher prices with the tariff channel as the main leg pressing the other way. The 2018 round is the base rate: prices fell then, with the season-average farm price dropping from $9.33/bu [N87] to $8.48/bu [N88].

## Mechanism
The tariff channel is high-confidence in the driver model and one-signed for this contract: Chinese duties on US-origin beans reroute demand to Brazil, pressuring the US-Gulf-linked Chicago benchmark while Brazilian premiums firm. It works through export pace -- a slow US sales pace is the model's readable symptom, and it feeds the stocks-to-use ratio, which is the high-confidence price link (lower ratio, higher price). Two of the four conditions the trade-war demand-loss pattern names are showing here -- the lagging export pace and Chinese reserves -- which is at its stated threshold; the pattern is price-pressuring.

What stops that from dominating is the buffer. A 10.72% stocks-to-use ratio [N54] at the 23rd percentile [N56] is a thin cushion, and thin cushions make supply or demand shocks convex to the upside while capping the downside from a demand loss. Offsetting the tariff leg: the crush margin at 2.6 USD/bu [N60], the 92nd percentile of its own record [N62], pulls bean demand forward at high confidence -- a domestic demand channel the tariff does not touch. Managed money is at 241,501 contracts [N31], the 99th percentile [N41]: that amplifies moves and flags reversal risk, not a cause.

## The record
Dated sequence, as the corpus carries it:
- China imposed 25 percent duties on US beans in spring 2018 and prices dropped significantly [E1]; the specific duty took effect 6 July 2018, 25% on top of the normal 3% [E2], and USDA flagged the trade effect on 12 July 2018 [E3].
- Chinese offtake halved across that marketing year: 27,682 thousand MT in MY2017 [N10] to 13,370 in MY2018 [N11], from 36,148 in MY2016 [N12].
- The price effect showed inside the same crop year, not with a long lag -- the model's 0-2 quarter lag ran fast. The November 2018 Chicago soybean contract settled 1,042 US cents/bushel on 3 April 2018 [N20], 930.5 by 15 June 2018 [N22], 894.5 on 6 July 2018 [N23] and 844.25 by 4 September 2018 [N24], recovering to 870.5 by 14 November 2018 [N25]. The season-average farm price fell from $9.33/bu in MY2017/18 [N87] to $8.48/bu in MY2018/19 [N88].
- Relief came by policy, not by market healing: China's tariff-exclusion process from 2 March 2020 cut effective duties from 30.5 percent back to 3 percent [E23][E24], following a first exclusion round announced 18 February 2020 [E26].
- The channel reopened in 2025: Beijing placed retaliatory tariffs on US soybeans, reported 19 March 2025 [E7], with 10 to 15 percent more on US farm goods and 10 percent on soybeans announced February 2025.

This year's readings: China holds 9,530 thousand MT outstanding for MY2026 [N26] against 5 thousand MT for MY2025 [N27]; US exports are 41,368,000 MT for MY2025/26 [N5] with ending stocks 8,845,000 MT [N6], against 51,495,000 MT exported in MY2024/25 [N8]. USDA projects 45,858,000 MT of exports for MY2026/27 [N28] -- a projection, not an actual. The November 2026 Chicago contract settled 1,328 US cents/bushel on 21 September 2026 [N29] versus the November 2025 contract at 1,012 on 23 September 2025 [N30]. One dated-lag caveat: the newest document behind this page is 19 March 2025, so the 2026 tariff state is carried by the number rows, not by fresh text.

Where the record disagrees with the simple tariff story: in 2018 the loss of Chinese demand met a looser sheet and price fell [N88]; this year the same demand loss meets a stocks-to-use ratio at the 23rd percentile [N56], and the price tape is higher year-on-year vs. Same driver, different buffer -- that is the whole read.

## Where the record disagrees
The board's loud drivers lean both ways and I will name both legs. Price-pressuring: the lagging export pace, Brazilian exports at 118 MMT [N42], the 99th percentile of that record [N44], US harvested area at 34.76 M ha [N69] at the 91st percentile [N71], and Argentine production at 50 MMT [N63]. Price-supportive: the tight stocks-to-use ratio at high confidence, the crush margin at high confidence, and Argentine export policy read on exports of 6.45 MMT [N78] -- also high confidence. The high-confidence supportive legs outnumber the high-confidence pressuring one, which is why I lean up; the supply-glut pattern shows only two of the three conditions it names, short of its threshold.

On the climate leg, the tropical Pacific sea-surface anomaly reads +1.8 degC for July 2026 [N33], the 93rd percentile of its own record [N35], rising eight months running. This is one series read under two phase names, and the warm phase is the one in force -- on Chicago soybeans that phase is declared to move price the opposite way, a medium-confidence price-pressuring leg whose stated one-to-two-quarter window, counted from the run's start in November 2025, already closed on 30 May 2026. The comparable past state was September 2023; from that state Argentine production moved 0 MMT at the near end of the declared band [N81] and 2.9 MMT at the far end [N82] -- history on a single ranked case, not a forecast, and the corpus holds no dated document explaining that state.

## What to watch
- **Chinese reserve stocks** [N45], beginning stocks at 44.36 MMT for 2026, in the top decile of that record : this is one of the two conditions putting the trade-war demand-loss pattern at its threshold. Next print 9 October 2026. It reads wrong if the print returns the series to the middle of its own record.
- **The crush margin** [N57], 2.6 USD/bu read through 21 August 2026, 92nd percentile [N59]: the domestic demand leg that offsets the lost Chinese pull, acting over its declared window of 20 August to 20 November 2026. It reads wrong if the next print falls back to mid-record.
- **Weekly export sales** [N66], 622.69 thousand MT for 10 September 2026, 43rd percentile [N68] but rising two weeks running, acting over 10 September to 10 December 2026. Next print 24 September 2026. It reads wrong if the pace stalls again rather than continuing to recover -- that would confirm the tariff channel is biting the balance sheet rather than merely the origin split.
- **The stocks-to-use ratio** [N54], 10.72%, three marketing years falling, next print 9 October 2026: this is the buffer that makes the upside convex. It reads wrong if the print turns back above the tight line or the run breaks.
- **The Pacific sea-surface anomaly** [N33], +1.8 degC, eight months rising, next print 1 October 2026, with its declared window opening 31 October 2026 and closing 31 January 2027. It reads wrong if the print turns back inside the strong line or the run breaks.

One note on coverage: the front delivery month could not be named on this session, so every price above is quoted as a named delivery month, never as "the price."
